subject: Priority rules for reserved GPU preemption — Aurora case
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Date: Tue, 12 Oct 2027 09:03:00 -0700
Subject: Priority rules for reserved GPU preemption — Aurora case

Team,

Aurora (related to DEAL-3482-AUR) just went into a sustained burst across their dedicated pool overnight — sustained 3x token/sec for ~6 hours. Their reserved tranche is 20% of the north-virginia dedicated capacity and the surge is encroaching on other reserved customers (notably Lumina Labs). We need a short, defensible policy recommendation that balances: (1) contractual commitments, (2) latency SLOs for higher-tier customers, (3) minimizing noisy neighbor impact, and (4) commercial remedies (credits / short-term capacity).

Attached: preemption_draft_v2.pdf (policy draft), aurora_capacity_report_Q3.xlsx (usage heatmap).

Please reply with concrete options (technical thresholds + commercial mitigation) by EOD Oct 15 so I can escalate to Sales leadership and Legal for signoff. High-level options to consider:
- Strict reserved (no preemption) for accounts with a contractual guarantee (fastest from a retention POV but blows out burst capacity).
- Tiered lanes with a soft preemption window: SLO-guaranteed lane (no preempt) + burst lane (best-effort, soft-evict after X minutes).
- Active preemption with credits: allow up to Y% preemption during sustained surges in exchange for a one-time credit / temporary concession.

Key constraints from infra: we must avoid mass OOM/kv-cache thrashing when preempting GPUs — that drives P99 regressions. Karthik, can you quantify latency impact and a safe preempt cadence (min eviction window, drain strategy)? Monica, think through what concessions we can offer Aurora without setting a precedent. Marissa, any runbook updates required for SRE?

Thanks,
Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Head of Capacity Strategy, Redwood Inference

Attachments: preemption_draft_v2.pdf (20 pages, policy draft), aurora_capacity_report_Q3.xlsx (Excel, 2 sheets)

Subject: Re: Priority rules for reserved GPU preemption — Aurora case

Vivek — quick technical readout and options. TL;DR: safe preemption is possible but must be done at the request level with graceful KV cache handoff and a throttled drain window (we estimate ~45–120s extra latency on affected requests during eviction windows).

Observed: Aurora’s jobs are long-context chat workloads with large KV footprints. Immediate preemption without cache migration causes P95 increases of up to 2.1x in our staging tests (when >40% of a node's KV is migrated).

Proposal (technical):
1) Tiered lanes:
   - Guaranteed lane (G): pinned GPUs, no preemption.
   - Burst lane (B): best-effort; can be throttled/backfilled.
2) Soft preemption window: only evict from B after sustained >15m over the burst threshold; eviction executed as a graceful drain where we:
   - Mark instance for drain, stop accepting new sessions for 30s, flush KV to a short-lived cache store, spin up replacement on different node, and rehydrate with best-effort (expected client-visible latency spike during rehydrate: +0.7s median, +2.0s P95 for affected requests).
3) Hard preemption cap: never preempt more than 30% of a single customer’s active nodes in a 1h window to avoid cascade effects.
4) Canary fallback: route 5% of traffic to smaller model-variant (quantized) if preemption would violate latency SLOs.

Impact model: I will attach a simple CSV (capacity_impact_model.csv) with expected token cost delta and P95 changes across preemption levels. Commercially relevant numbers: under soft preemption we expect a ~6–12% loss in effective tokens/sec for customers in burst lane during sustained events.

If we go with active preemption + credit, we must build an automation guardrail: auto-disable preemption for accounts with pending renewals within 60 days unless approved by GTM.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Director, Serving Runtime

Thanks — adding the commercial lens. A few notes: 
1) Aurora's renewal window opens in 28 days and they currently have an enterprise discount tied to annual commit. We should avoid a public 'preempt' label in the contract.
2) Options we can offer, ranked:
   A) Short-term committed uplift: offer +10 reserved GPUs for 90 days at a discounted uplift price (this preserves long-term retention and buys time).
   B) Preemption + credit: allow temporary preemption with a 10% monthly credit for the surge month and a clear clause that preemption is limited to the burst lane and capped at 30% of their active nodes in any 1h window.
   C) No-preempt (only if they sign additional reserved capacity or raise to a higher SLA tier).

Suggested customer email (short):
"We propose a temporary mitigation: Redwood will place Aurora into a tiered availability plan (guaranteed lane + burst lane). During sustained surges we may route some burst traffic to best-effort capacity; if preemption occurs, Redwood will apply a one-time credit for the month and prioritize migration to additional reserved GPUs upon next billing cycle."

Legal: need to craft language that avoids establishing preemption as a standard right for all customers. Also get Sales leadership to ok the credit.

-Monica
Monica Patel
Head of Commercial Operations

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica_patel@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Sylvia Chen <sylvia@aurora.ai>
Cc: Rajiv Gupta <rajiv@luminallabs.com>
Date: Thu, 14 Oct 2027 14:15:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Priority rules for reserved GPU preemption — Aurora case

Sylvia — looping you in with a concrete, short-term plan so we can align before escalations grow. Karthik and Monica have run the technical and commercial tradeoffs; below is the proposal Redwood would like Aurora to approve for the next 90 days. If acceptable, we will operationalize immediately and follow with a customer-facing doc.

Proposed 90-day mitigation (effective immediately upon sign):
- We will move Aurora workloads into a two-lane model: Guaranteed lane (your critical production routes) + Burst lane (best-effort, used for experimental/overflow traffic).
- Only traffic routed to the Burst lane is eligible for preemption. Preemption rules: soft-evict after 15 minutes of sustained over-threshold activity; never preempt more than 30% of Aurora's active nodes in any 1h window.
- If preemption occurs for >3 sustained events in a 30-day window, Redwood will apply a 10% credit for that month's invoice and prioritize an uplift of reserved GPUs per commercial agreement.
- Technical safeguards: graceful drain (30s stop-accept + KV spill + rehydrate), canary fallback to a smaller quantized variant for up to 5% traffic during peak to maintain latency.

We will track incidents in JIRA INF-6121 and share daily heatmap snapshots to the linked Drive folder. If you prefer a different split between guaranteed and burst lanes, we can model the cost/latency impact.

Please confirm by EOD Oct 15 whether Aurora accepts this temporary mitigation or if you want to schedule a short call to discuss alternatives. If we do not hear back, we'll hold the plan pending formal sign-off (we will not enact preemption without your approval unless there is an active SLA breach affecting other customers).

Thanks,
Vivek

Vivek / team — thanks for the fast work and the clear proposal. We appreciate the two-lane approach; however, two requests before we can agree: 
1) We need a firm guarantee that any production route we mark as Guaranteed lane will not be preempted under the temporary plan. Can you provide a short appendix that lists the exact API routes and matching conditions so our engineering team can validate?
2) We would prefer the 10% credit to be applied automatically for the first qualifying month without requiring an escalation.

We are open to the uplift of reserved GPUs, but need a clear timeline (provisioning within 10 business days after acceptance). Can we jump on a 30-minute call Monday to finalize the guaranteed-route list?

Sylvia Chen
VP of Platform Engineering, AuroraAI
